toc.title: What the safety words are for
Doubt and judgment are part of it
What to do with the doubt

blocks.p: I want to talk about the process of change, including doubt, self-judgment, and evaluating yourself. I think this can help you get some clarity on your own process of getting unstuck, so you can keep focusing on getting unstuck.
This question came from someone taking one of my courses:

q: Hi there, Justin. This is connected to safety words. I'm in my safe environment. There's just me. I'm revisiting the safety words tonight and feel slightly different to when I first explored the safety words.

The words loved, compassion, validated, understood, empathy, and affection stand out, but each of those words in my head is followed with self. ... I only feel those words because I am here for myself. My question is, is this okay, or am I closing myself off? It feels okay to me, I think. Thanks for any thoughts coming my way.

blocks.h: What the safety words are for

blocks.p: First, what is this person talking about?

Safety is not just the literal environment, the place you're actually in. It's not just the people around you. That isn't what we mean by safety. Through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory, safety refers to biological pathways. We're talking about biology.

In that course, I put together a list of safety words for participants to reference throughout. Not just once, not just at the end, but throughout, to check in about their experiences and get some conscious awareness of anything new developing within them.

There's a felt sense, a present moment experience we have with our biology, and it's super easy to miss. Until we actually slow down and notice it, we might just keep missing it. So it helps to consciously slow down, look at a list of words, and ask, "Have I felt this recently?" Or this week, or whatever pace you're on.

The words this person named, loved, compassion, validated, understood, empathy, and affection, are just a small sampling of that list. But you may never ask yourself, "Do I feel validated? Do I feel compassion or empathy? Do I feel affection?" How often do you ask yourself that?

When you're prompted to ask, it gives you a moment to look and say, "Have I actually felt validated this week? What led me to those feelings, and how can I reproduce that?" That's a prompt to build on it: to build feelings of safety, or to build the safety anchors that lead to them.

It's hard to dive into something without knowing at least some checkpoints or milestones. If you don't know what safety is, you may miss it when it's there. So you need something to prompt you to recognize safety when it's actually there. Hopefully that's something we therapists do with our clients: noticing that over the past week, there were moments they felt safe, or connected, or things were different in some way. But you have to be prompted to look.

It's not an endpoint, because I don't think the work is ever done. Hopefully we're always changing and growing and challenging ourselves. It's more like a checkpoint: did I feel these things or not? Which of these words did I feel, and how is that different from the past?

Even "checkpoint" isn't a great word, because everybody's experience of getting unstuck is different from the next person's. There isn't one path that works for everybody. So maybe the safety words are more like a marker, or an illustration of safety developing.

Getting unstuck, making change in your life, is absolutely a process. It's not a one-time thing. It's not like we shake and tremble and the trauma is released, or our nervous system is reset. That's not the way it works. I have not seen it that way, and I have not experienced it that way.

We're constantly building our capacity to feel safe and to stay in our safety state. In episode 135, Safety Cue Dependency, I talked about this: the process of building safety versus applying safety as medicine.
Getting unstuck isn't just an issue of changing your thoughts. You have to change your biological state first. Story follows state.

It isn't just an issue of changing behavior, either. Our behavior stems from the potential of our biology. If our biology is primed to connect with others, our behavior will follow. If our biology is prepped for running away, our behavior will match that.

Change also has somatic pieces. It involves the body, and that's something we neglect very often. I don't just mean how we feel. I also mean biological mechanisms like the vagal brake, which is the influence of the safe and social state on the heart. It keeps the heart beating at a calmer pace. Building the capacity to feel safe really means building the strength of the vagal brake: the ability of our social engagement system to tolerate higher and higher levels of distress.

Change and getting unstuck require patience. It's not one and done. There are absolutely going to be obstacles, and you need patience to get through them. You have to be able to see that there is hope, and that improvement is happening, not just that it will happen, but that it is happening, in little pieces, little doses at a time.

There's really no right way to make change. Even in a course that lays out a flow I recommend, your experience of that flow can be different from the next person's. And whatever your avenue for getting unstuck is, there's no one right way.

Maybe your thing is yoga, and the movement helps you. Maybe the co-regulative pieces of being around other people who are safe, encouraging, and supportive are fundamental to your process of change. I can't tell you that's wrong. I can't tell you any one approach is right or wrong for anybody.

Every one of us is going to go through something different in terms of what helps us. There are a lot of similarities, of course, but I don't think there's one correct technique, one correct path, or one correct way of thinking. The stories that pop into our minds, the feelings, the intensities of making change and getting unstuck: they're different for every one of us, and that's really cool.

So it takes patience, but it also takes curiosity: being interested in what change feels like for you, what safety feels like for you, what meeting your goals looks and feels like. Be patient, and notice all the little bumps and bruises along the way, or what seem like bumps and bruises but are really just the process of change.

blocks.h: Doubt and judgment are part of it

blocks.p: There are going to be obstacles. You're going to have self-doubt. You're going to have judgment. You're going to evaluate your progress. That's not inherently bad, but we can easily become evaluative in a very negative way toward ourselves. That's where judgment and blame come into play.

Doubting yourself and judging yourself is not a failure. It's absolutely part of the process of making change in anyone's life. The issue is: are you getting sucked into it, or are you noticing it and using it to your advantage?
Judgment and doubt are completely normal parts of getting unstuck, wherever you're at in life. Here's why.

As we climb the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), we'll drop back down into more of a defensive state, because feeling safe can be extremely uncomfortable for many people. If you're not used to it, and all of a sudden you start feeling trust and vulnerability, or you're making eye contact with a therapist and you notice it, just feeling these things can be really uncomfortable. It can send you right back down your polyvagal ladder into a more defensive state. That can happen even if you're not aware of it.

And as you drop back down the ladder, story follows state. Your thoughts change along with your state. You're going to have judgments and doubt. You're going to evaluate yourself and the situation. None of these are inherently wrong. It's just part of the process.

It's the same in the other direction. As you access more safety, you'll have more positivity in your thinking, more social connection in your behavior, more empathy in your feelings, more generally positive feelings. That's a much different experience. Trust and vulnerability are weird if you're not used to them. They're very uncomfortable, and they can send you right back down the ladder. So you have to get used to them.

When I say get used to them, I don't mean forcing yourself to make eye contact with someone until you get used to it. I mean continually putting yourself in situations where you feel more and more safety, calm, or connection, or just being present in your body in the present moment. The more you do that mindfully, the more you build the strength of your safety state, your social engagement system. What I'm describing is your window of tolerance, or your vagal brake: the ability of the social engagement system to keep the heartbeat at a calmer pace even when things get difficult.

Along with this climbing and descending as things get challenging, it's very possible to have evaluations or judgmental thoughts. "Is this okay? Am I doing this right? Is this going to work?" Very normal. And it probably comes from some discomfort, some more defensive feelings, from accessing your own safety state and then dropping right back down the ladder.

blocks.h: What to do with the doubt

blocks.p: If you can notice the thoughts, that's awesome. I think it's exactly where you need to be. Then you can go further:

ol: Notice the thought. "Am I doing this right?" "Is it okay to feel this way?" "Is it okay to focus on myself?"

Notice the feeling that comes with it. It's not just a thought. Our thoughts follow our state, but between our polyvagal state and our conscious awareness of our thoughts, there may be some feelings. If your thought is "I think I'm doing this wrong," the feeling might be nervousness, concern, worry, or anxiety.

Notice what that feeling feels like in your body. What does it feel like to be nervous? To be unsure? To have anxiety? Those feelings live somewhere in your body. That's what I mean by somatic sensations.

blocks.p: Noticing the thought: awesome. Noticing the feeling that comes along with it: fantastic. Noticing what those emotions feel like in your body is the step after that.
Then give yourself some top-down validation and normalization.
Validate it: yes, this is difficult.

And normalize it. You may have decades' worth of conditioning on a very biological level. At the time, I worked with kids during the day and adults at night, and those adults had literally decades' worth of conditioning: being stuck in a traumatized state, living in family dynamics that conditioned them toward a more defensive state. Coming out of that, and having it feel okay, is a challenge. That's completely normal. Depending on someone's context, and how long they've been in it, it may take a while to come out of it and build the strength of the vagal brake, the strength of the safety state. That's okay.

It's like asking someone who doesn't run to run a mile in a really fast time. I don't know what a normal mile time is, so fill in the blank. It's not realistic for someone who hasn't practiced, who isn't a runner.
You have to put the work in first and build your ability. Then you keep doing it to improve your time. Then you keep going to maintain it.
It's the same with the safety state. I don't expect anyone who hasn't practiced being in a safety state to suddenly feel it and be able to maintain it. That's not a realistic expectation.

So recognizing these thoughts, and the feelings and somatic sensations that come along with them, is a really good thing. It's actually a good sign, because it shows there's more safety in your system.

If you're present enough to notice, "Am I doing this right?", that's a hell of a lot different than dwelling on how terrible you are: "I suck so much. I'm going to be stuck my whole life. I can never change." Noticing the thought, and then noticing the feeling that comes with it, is different. You're not getting sucked into it. You're recognizing it and using it to your advantage, to look a little deeper, to be curious and explore the inner world you have.

In therapy, when my clients and I check in on how the past week went, what was different, what's going well, and what still needs work, a lot of times they'll say something like: "My presenting problem, my anger or my numbness, was still there, but it was different. I was able to recognize it and be with it. It didn't spiral out of control. I was able to be more present in the moment, in my body. The problem's not 100% fixed, but I was able to stay aware of that moment, feel those feelings, and then handle it."

Oftentimes they handle it in a different way. At the very least, it doesn't spiral out of control like it used to. That's not perfect. The work's not done yet. But it shows there's more safety in the system, more capacity to be with their feelings and not get sucked into those defensive feelings.
